text.p: Former Wimbledon champion John McEnroe is "embarrassed" by the state of modern tennis and believes drastic measures are required to boost the sport's fading popularity.

McEnroe chose a damp third day at the All England Club on Wednesday to attack the tennis establishment who he believes are guilty of ignoring deep-rooted problems which have led to a growing lack of real personalities in the game.
"Something has to be done and I think drastic changes would be far preferable," said McEnroe, now an outspoken commentator with an American television network.
"I'm embarrassed by this sport right now. We've lost a tremendous amount of forward momentum. It's very evident that tennis is losing popularity, not just in America but also in England and Japan."

McEnroe, who won the last of his three Wimbledon titles in 1984, is convinced tennis should follow the more aggressive marketing techniques pioneered by American basketball and insists world number one Pete Sampras should play a more active role in promoting his sport.
"It's not only about hitting the ball over the net," said McEnroe, currently taking a break from Wimbledon to perform with his rock band in Spain.
"Pete doesn't have to act like I behaved on centre court, but I think it's important the players lead the way and do far more than they're doing now.

"Pete is a fine player, but there are many players making more money than they should do. There are a number of guys at Wimbledon who have no business being in the tournament. It's bad for the sport if guys are just turning up to collect a pay cheque."

There is nothing to match McEnroe's famous rivalry with Bjorn Borg in the men's game at present, and the New Yorker is cruelly accurate when he points out that most of the world's top players, bar the likes of Andre Agassi and Boris Becker, "can walk down the main street and not be stopped."
Significantly, former champion Chris Evert believes McEnroe's sentiments can broadly be applied to the women's game as well.

"I'm not impressed with the standard," commented Evert, reflecting on the rapid rise of world number one Martina Hingis and the surprise triumph of Croatia's Iva Majoli at the French Open earlier this month.
"Steffi (Graf) was a better number one five years ago and Martina (Navratilova) was a better one 10 years ago. It's disappointing the way things have panned out."
Even Anna Kournikova, the 16-year-old Russian prodigy who made a startling Wimbledon centre court debut on Tuesday, has yet to impress Evert, who won three Wimbledon titles between 1974 and 1981.

"She hasn't convinced me mentally. She doesn't know how to orchestrate a point yet. I never want to build a player up too much because it usually spells disaster. She's got a model face, a great body and she's marketable, but there's more to it than that."

Both Evert and McEnroe believe a retractable roof would help ease Wimbledon's perennial problems with the weather and guarantee more action for the long-suffering supporters who queued for hours in the rain on Wednesday just to obtain a glimpse of the famous Centre Court.

McEnroe also advocates an end to formal press conferences which have become notorious for the lack of insight offered by the players, and wants the authorities to force the top players to do more individual interviews to project themselves better.
Top of his own list is Becker, who can expect a request for an in-depth chat with his old adversary in the next few days.
McEnroe, confident he can persuade the German champion to open his heart, revealed: "I'm going to tell him he's a jerk if he doesn't."
